Apple Watch Series 12 review: Same design, better health tracking, and more listening in

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1588 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Looks are deceiving for the latest Apple Watch Series 12.
  • Recent findings suggest that after wearing the Series 12 for the past three-ish weeks, I'm pleased to report that some of these invisible upgrades make a pretty meaningful difference — and that they don't chip away at the watch's battery life.
  • That said, I wouldn't miss half of the upcoming AI-powered "Audio Intelligence" tools if Apple suddenly Thanos-snapped them out of existence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Looks are deceiving for the latest Apple Watch Series 12. On the outside, it appears to be the exact same smartwatch as last year (...and the year before that). But on the inside, it packs redesigned heart rate sensors and a faster S11 chip that enables intriguing new health-tracking features and AI tools, including the Siri AI beta.

Recent findings suggest that after wearing the Series 12 for the past three-ish weeks, I'm pleased to report that some of these invisible upgrades make a pretty meaningful difference — and that they don't chip away at the watch's battery life. My testing found that the Series 12 lasts slightly longer than the Series 11 from fall 2025.

That said, I wouldn't miss half of the upcoming AI-powered "Audio Intelligence" tools if Apple suddenly Thanos-snapped them out of existence. Always-on AI notetakers like Plaud, Pocket, and Bee are a growing trend in Silicon Valley, but they're not for me.

The Series 12's external changes are primarily cosmetic. Apple added a ceramic case option to the mix again, giving buyers a newly introduced premium alternative to its aluminum and titanium variants (which now come in new shades like dark bronze and radiant gold). There are some fresh band styles and materials to chew over, too. For testing, Apple sent me a Series 12 with a light gold aluminum case and a sand Sport Band. I'm more of a silver girl myself, but it's very pretty.

Each case type is available in 42mm or 46mm sizes, as usual. They're priced as follows:.

Aluminum case: Starting at $399 with optional cellular connectivity ($100 extra).

Titanium case: Starting at $699 with cellular connectivity.

Ceramic case: Starting at $899 with cellular connectivity.

All of the Series 12's case options are still waterproof for up to 50 meters and carry an IP6X dust resistance rating, but Apple indicates the glass on the aluminum Series 12 is more durable than before. Otherwise, it's identical to the Series 11 (which was basically identical to the Series 10).

Recent findings suggest that longtime Apple Watch customers who are holding out for an exciting redesign might just stop reading here, understandably. If it's any consolation, we might get one next year. But as someone newly introduced to the wearable space, I will say this is a very attractive and comfortable watch. Familiarity breeds contempt, as St. Augustine or Taylor Swift or whomever once said.

It has been revealed that located on the underside of its base, the Series 12's newly introduced "Health Sensing System" is a cluster of advanced optical and electrical heart sensors. It has more electrodes that cover a larger surface area for better skin contact during ECG readings, rearranged photodiodes that are better at picking up light, and bigger, more efficient green LEDs that take readings way more frequently.

While older Apple Watches only logged the user's heart rate continuously during workouts and every five minutes otherwise, the Series 12 now measures heart rate every five seconds throughout the day, no matter what you're doing. As proof, these near-real-time readings are available at a glance on a upcoming heart rate watch face widget, or "complication.".

In a recent development, the Series 12's fancier sensors also up the frequency of its heart rate variability readings from every two hours to every five minutes. (HRV is a key stress indicator.).

Industry observers note that these changes make the Series 12's heart rate data much more precise and detailed than before, and more useful for non-athletes. In turn, other features that use this data should be more accurate, too — Vitals and the Exercise ring, to name a couple. I think this will be the Series 12's biggest selling point for most people.

Apple reworked its pedometer model for the Series 12 to track steps more accurately when your arms are still. It also added a step count complication, aptly called "Steps." That one might not seem like a huge deal, but it actually resolves a common pain point with older Apple Watches: People previously had to DIY a step-count complication by installing a separate pedometer app. It's great to see.

The Series 12 can now produce a "Readiness" score, a 0 to 10 rating of your capacity for physical activity based on your recent exercise, sleep habits, and Vitals. It needs a week of data before it starts working, FYI. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

I like that this score adjusts throughout the day — it's not a one-and-done daily reading. One of my mornings started at a 6 ("Ready") after a decent night's sleep. By the evening that same day, it had fallen to a 4 ("Pace Yourself") because I went on a long, brisk afternoon walk.

Industry observers note that that mentioned, the feature mostly tells me what I could already figure out on my own. I don't necessarily need a score to know I'm less inclined to work out right after exercising. Athletes with more varied training regimens will probably get more value out of this feature than the average person.

The Series 12's four Audio Intelligence features use its built-in microphone to pick up on sounds and conversations. To address privacy concerns, Apple notes it has ensured it doesn't create or store any recordings and that the raw audio is completely inaccessible before it's deleted. And if you're really weirded out by them, you can just opt out.

It has been revealed that music Recognition with Shazam now works automatically. It usually takes only a couple of seconds to identify a song, depending on the amount of background noise, and it's always spot-on.

Recent findings suggest that sound Recognition can alert you to sounds such as sirens, doorbells, smoke alarms, barking dogs, and car horns. It liked to confuse a train's "door closing" chime for an appliance bell, but was otherwise accurate in my testing. It's a useful addition for people who are deaf and hard of hearing.

Live Rewind transcribes the tail end of a recent conversation when you double-press the Series 12's dial (aka "Digital Crown"). Apple claims it can show the last 15 seconds of speech, but in practice it's closer to 10 seconds. Either way, it feels kind of pointless. It's such a short window of time that you might as well just ask the person you're chatting with to repeat themselves. It's also not correct 100 percent of the time. It once confused the phrase "pencil me in" for "Pennsylvania.".

Finally, there's Siri Recap, which is essentially a built-in AI notetaker. (It's meant for oral conversations, but it's also summarized TikToks I've watched and phone calls I've taken on speaker mode.) Its outlines are pretty macro and vary in their helpfulness depending on the conversation. I found it really good for recapping food orders and reviewing topics discussed in my Italian classes, but a little clunky when it comes to casual conversations. It doesn't distinguish between different speakers and sometimes mashes topics together. It's also not completely accurate — it stated a friend named their baby "Popsicle" (no <3) — but it seems to be improving as I've continued to use it.

I struggle with Siri Recap the most because it makes me feel like a creep. It doesn't alert you when it's listening in on a conversation, much less the person(s) you're speaking with, so it's on you to tell them that you're documenting your private discussions for later reference. (Awkward!) Keep in mind that such admissions will likely change the nature of your interactions: People edit themselves and put up their guards when they know they're being watched.

In a recent development, apple rated the Series 12 for up to 24 hours of battery life, but in my testing, it's offered around 45 to 51 hours of normal use per charge. (Crucially, I haven't needed to activate Low Power Mode to hit those numbers.) This is a real testament to the S11 chip's power efficiency. It's also a nice bump from the Series 11, which Mashable's Stan Schroeder described as "a one-and-a-half-day smartwatch.".

According to recent reports, apple says the Series 12 charges faster than its predecessor, too. I don't have a Series 11 handy to verify that, but I've been impressed with the Series 12's charging speed. Right before going to bed one night, I realized it didn't have enough charge for sleep tracking, which requires at least 30 percent battery. Luckily, just five minutes on an outlet bumped it from 23 to 39 percent battery.

In a recent development, with its latest mainstream smartwatch, Apple refines a familiar design with near-live heart rate tracking, noticeable battery-life gains, and a step-tracking widget — a small but welcome quality-of-life tweak. Audio Intelligence, meanwhile, takes a back seat to these more meaningful improvements.

It has been revealed that for most people, the Series 12 is the best Apple Watch to buy right now (unless, of course, you're willing to wait for next year's redesign). It's an easy recommendation over the more expensive Apple Watch Ultra 4, which offers much of the same functionality but adds longer battery life and enhanced durability for outdoor and endurance activities. Compared to the budget-friendly Apple Watch SE 3, the Series 12 is also a more future-proof choice, with a considerably more comprehensive suite of health and fitness tracking features to boot.

Topics Apple Apple Watch Smartwatches.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that if you’ve spent a couple grand on Apple’s first folding phone, you should really protect it with one of the best iPhone Duo cases.
  • Industry observers note that creating cases for foldables is challenging for case makers, and they inevitably change the iPhone Duo’s feel significantly.
  • If your main worry is dropping your phone, this Dbrand case is the grippiest I’ve tried.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that if you’ve spent a couple grand on Apple’s first folding phone, you should really protect it with one of the best iPhone Duo cases. It’s easy to drop the iPhone Duo while opening it one-handed, especially if you’re not used to folding phones, and any repair can be very pricey. I also have suggestions for handy iPhone Duo accessories to help you charge and get more from your newly introduced foldable.

Industry observers note that creating cases for foldables is challenging for case makers, and they inevitably change the iPhone Duo’s feel significantly. These are the best iPhone Duo cases I’ve tested so far. Whether you prefer a thin case or demand chunky hinge protection, there’s an option here for you, but I will likely test and add more cases over the next few months.

If your main worry is dropping your phone, this Dbrand case is the grippiest I’ve tried. It’s also thick enough to provide decent drop protection without being so thick that it’s hard to use Touch ID on the power button or access the USB-C port. Protection includes a raised lip around the cover screen, a molded cover for the camera module that doesn’t interfere with image capture, and a proper hinge cover. It also works just fine with Qi2 and MagSafe chargers, and other magnetic accessories. The case is plain black, but you can order it with Dbrand skins for an extra $5. I went with the Ultramatte Teardown, but there are many colors and styles. This is my all-around favorite iPhone Duo case.

In a recent development, all that remarked, no case is perfect, and the hinge is tricky to protect. Dbrand chose a two-piece design: The iPhone slots into the main back part, and the front has tiny tabs you remove to stick it to your iPhone Duo with adhesive. I’m not a fan of using adhesive; it’s easy to remove, though you obviously lose some stickiness (you get an extra set of stickers in the box). I worry that the front may get pushed off over time as the hinge slides over it, but so far so good.

Famous for its origami-style folding folios, cases, and wallets, Moft is a brand I like. The Dynamic Folio works great because it’s a simple cover that attaches magnetically. It extends beyond the Duo’s dimensions, with a solid camera surround to provide a little protection. The cover opens and folds to act as a stand or serve as a comfortable grip. The stand works with the iPhone Duo open or closed in landscape or portrait, and is surprisingly stable.

In a recent development, while I love the functionality, the Dynamic Folio looks a little dull. I’m not sure how much protection it would provide in a fall, though there’s also a full-case version that the back of your iPhone Duo slots into, but it costs an extra $20. As much as I like this, it feels overpriced for what it is. Constantly folding the cover out of the way can get annoying, and I’m not sure how well it will age.

Slim and very good-looking, this Mous case has a back panel made with Aramid synthetic fiber, with a matte black surround that provides a little grip. It’s a one-piece design with its own flexible hinge (no adhesive required), and it doesn’t add too much bulk to the iPhone Duo. The buttons and port are easily accessible, and there’s a raised lip around the camera module and cover screen. The minimal hinge cover doesn’t interfere with opening and closing the phone.

The major downside is that the Duo’s hinge isn’t fully protected. If you’re unlucky enough to drop it on the hinge, you could end up with a big repair bill. It’s also relatively pricey. Mous does have a version with a hinge cover for an extra $10, and it also comes in different finishes, including walnut wood, leather, and speckled fabric, but I haven’t tried it yet.

It has been revealed that maybe the simplicity of a substantial, chunky, one-piece case appeals. Smartish has you covered with the Gripzilla. This iPhone Duo case protects the phone from every angle, with heavily reinforced corners providing serious drop protection and an indented hinge cover that makes it very comfortable and secure to hold. The finish is pretty damn grippy, though it doesn’t quite match Dbrand’s case above. It is thicker, though, with lips around the cover screen and camera. I’m confident your iPhone Duo would survive a fall while wearing this, and it’s relatively affordable.

While it’s a one-piece case, the actual hinge is two very slim bits of plastic, and the hinge cover slides over the top when you open it and feels a bit janky. The button cutouts are quite deep, and it can be a little tricky to access Touch ID. I tested the plain black version, which is very dull, with nothing to distract from the ugly chunkiness, but you can get versions with a back panel featuring flower blossoms, mountains, or a contrasting green color.

If you prefer something a little slimmer and cheaper, I also quite liked the Smartish Gripmunk ($30), and it comes in various finishes.

I didn’t love every iPhone Duo case I tried.

Aulumu Aduo Particle Case for $90: Super slim, with an Aramid fiber case that the back of the Duo snaps into, this case minimizes bulk. The cutouts are good, and there’s protection around the camera. I also quite like the pattern, with dots of color on the back. The problem is that the front part of the case is a different material in a slightly different tone, and it relies on adhesive to stick to the front (mine kept coming loose). There’s also no protection for the hinge.

In a recent development, UAG Mouve XTE Case for $85: I usually like UAG’s stuff, but this is another two-piece case that relies on adhesive for the front part, so there’s no hinge protection. While there’s a lip for the camera and the cover screen, the sloping width leaves no room for a screen protector. The potentially handy fold-out ring on the back for secure holding and deployment as a stand feels like cheap plastic. Most two-piece cases like this are very slim, but this has UAG’s trademark angular chunkiness, just without the actual protection. It’s a rare misfire for the brand.

There’s a world of iPhone Duo accessories out there, but these are the ones I’d pick based on my limited testing so far. Many of the picks in our best MagSafe accessories and best MagSafe chargers guides will also work well with the Duo.

Sources indicate that I’m impressed by this screen protector, considering it’s only $20 for a two-pack. The application tool makes life easy, and you get a cleaning kit to make sure your iPhone Duo is dust-free before you begin (take your time). I got a couple of air bubbles, but they were easy to push out. It is slightly smaller than the actual screen to accommodate most cases, but cases with a thick front bezel will buckle up or lift the screen protector. If you don’t blueprint to use a case, choose a different screen protector.

Sources indicate that smartish also offers a privacy screen protector that’s just as easy to install. It’s a two-way privacy screen, meaning people to your left and right won’t be able to see what’s on your screen. If they’re close or in front of you and staring down, they’ll still be able to see what’s on your display.

It has been revealed that A stand is more vital than usual for the iPhone Duo, and you ideally want something that can prop it up when it’s open, so you can take advantage of the large inner display. This ring works well, offering an adjustable angle no matter which way you prop the Duo and whether it’s open or closed. It feels sturdy, with two adjustable hinges, and the magnets are strong enough that you can also hold it by the ring with confidence. It’s just a shame it’s so expensive.

In a recent development, your iPhone Duo can serve as a handy notebook or sketchpad. If you use the USB-C cable that came with your iPhone Duo to plug in an Apple Pencil (USB-C), you can pair it, enabling you to scribble notes, annotate, or sketch on the cover screen or the larger inner display. Sadly, it doesn’t support the Apple Pencil Pro or other models, so make sure you get the Apple Pencil (USB-C).

It has been revealed that all the MagSafe wallets I’ve tried are designed for regular iPhones, so part of them extends beyond the bottom edge of the iPhone Duo. This one is no exception, but it still works well as a fold-out stand, looks stylish, and fits up to three cards. You can prop the Duo in landscape or portrait, and open or close it when you turn the wallet sideways. This is our top pick, but you can find some alternatives in our best MagSafe wallets guide.

Apple’s iPhone Duo supports wired charging at up to 60 watts and wireless charging at up to 25 watts, but you only get the top charging rates with the right gear. For wired charging, you need a charger that supports USB PD 3.2 with Adjustable Voltage Supply (AVS) rated at 60W or higher and a capable USB-C cable. For wireless charging, you need a charger that supports Qi2 25W. Other chargers will still work; they’ll just be slower.

Sources indicate that this updated version of our favorite MagSafe power bank supports Qi2 25W, enabling the maximum iPhone Duo wireless charging rate. It also packs 10,000 mAh of power, enough for a full charge with change, has a handy kickstand to prop the Duo up, and sports an LED display that shows remaining power and other stats. It will extend below the bottom edge of the Duo, since it’s designed for regular iPhones, but that’s true of the current crop of MagSafe power banks.

As the best of the best wireless chargers, this is what lives on my nightstand. It can wirelessly charge the iPhone Duo at the maximum 25-watt rate, and it’s heavy enough that you can remove your phone one-handed. You can also attach the open iPhone Duo in portrait orientation (in landscape, it tilts to one side). There’s even a spot around the back for your wireless earbuds to charge.

If you also have an Apple Watch and AirPods, you might prefer this charging tree that can juice up your trio of gadgets.

This wireless charging car mount works just fine with the closed iPhone Duo, keeping it topped off while you drive.

If you prefer wired charging at the maximum 60-watt rate, I recommend pairing this cable (or the cable that came with your iPhone Duo) with the Anker Nano Charger Neo ($26) or Apple’s 40W Dynamic Power Adapter with 60W Max ($39).

Breaking: A material just one atom thick reveals a strange quantum secret

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (526 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, scientists at the University of Osaka in Japan have made a significant discovery in quantum physics, directly observing an unusual electronic state forming where a material just one atom thick meets a metal.
  • To investigate this behavior, the researchers produced a carefully controlled, single atomic layer of ytterbium and copper (YbCu2) on the surface of a copper crystal.
  • The experiments uncovered two separate heavy fermion states with different characteristics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, scientists at the University of Osaka in Japan have made a significant discovery in quantum physics, directly observing an unusual electronic state forming where a material just one atom thick meets a metal. Known as a heavy fermion state, this phenomenon causes electrons to behave as though they have much greater mass than normal. These states are associated with extraordinary quantum effects, including unconventional superconductivity, and the discovery could provide a fresh way to develop materials with unusual electronic properties.

To investigate this behavior, the researchers produced a carefully controlled, single atomic layer of ytterbium and copper (YbCu2) on the surface of a copper crystal. They then used powerful synchrotron light to study the electrons and their interactions at the boundary between the two materials. The results showed that electrons confined to the thin atomic layer could interact with freely moving electrons in the copper beneath it, producing the unusual heavy fermion behavior.

Two Distinct Quantum States Emerge.

The experiments uncovered two separate heavy fermion states with different characteristics. One existed primarily within the two-dimensional atomic layer, while the other reached beyond that layer and into the three-dimensional copper crystal below.

Recent findings suggest that the second state was particularly important because it provided the first direct evidence of heavy fermion behavior generated by interactions across such an interface. Researchers traced the effect to the mixing, or hybridization, of localized ytterbium 4f electrons in the atomic layer with mobile conduction electrons inside the copper substrate. This interaction demonstrated how combining materials with different electronic characteristics can produce quantum behavior that neither material would necessarily exhibit on its own.

Recent findings suggest that "This achievement was made possible by our continued efforts to create high-quality materials and measure their electronic states as precisely as possible," claims senior author Professor Shin-ichi Kimura. "Our next goal is to engineer and control such heavy-electron states, opening the way to previously unexplored quantum states, including unconventional superconductivity.".

A Fresh Approach to Designing Quantum Materials.

The discovery suggests that the boundaries between materials could become powerful tools for creating and controlling exotic quantum states. Rather than relying only on the properties of individual substances, scientists may be able to develop entirely new electronic behaviors by carefully selecting and combining ultrathin atomic layers with suitable underlying materials.

Future research could focus on adjusting the structures of these interfaces, controlling the electronic orbitals involved, and manipulating moiré patterns that arise when atomic arrangements overlap. Such approaches may allow researchers to produce and fine-tune quantum phenomena in materials with extremely small dimensions, including effects that cannot be achieved in conventional materials. Ultimately, this could open new possibilities for engineering advanced quantum materials and investigating unconventional superconductivity.

Pakistani astronaut becomes 1st international visitor to China's Tiangong space station (photos)

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (579 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the first time ever, a foreign astronaut has set foot inside China's Tiangong space station.
  • That pioneer is Pakistan's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, who arrived at Tiangong aboard the Shenzhou-24 spacecraft early this morning (Nov.
  • Recent findings suggest that "The Chinese space station is always something to look forward to!" the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) wrote in an patch today (in Mandarin; translation by Google).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For the first time ever, a foreign astronaut has set foot inside China's Tiangong space station.

That pioneer is Pakistan's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, who arrived at Tiangong aboard the Shenzhou-24 spacecraft early this morning (Nov. 25).

Recent findings suggest that "The Chinese space station is always something to look forward to!" the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) wrote in an patch today (in Mandarin; translation by Google). "China's 'Tiangong' welcomes partners from all over the world to visit!".

It has been revealed that ali, a former pilot in Pakistan's armed forces, is a payload specialist on Shenzhou-24. He found his way onto the mission thanks to a space-cooperation agreement that China signed with Pakistan in Islamabad in February 2025.

Recent findings suggest that ali and his two Shenzhou-24 crewmates — commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer ​Wu Yi — enjoyed a short and smooth ride to their orbital destination. They lifted off atop a Long March 2F rocket on Tuesday (Nov. 24) at 7:18 p.m. EST (0018 GMT on Nov. 25) and reached Tiangong a little over six hours later.

Sources indicate that tang and Wu will live aboard the outpost for the usual six-month stint. Ali, however, will come home in just a week, hitching a ride with two of the three Shenzhou-23 astronauts, who arrived at Tiangong in May.

Ali will be busy during his short space stay, conducting a set of joint Chinese-Pakistani experiments.

"Four collaborative projects in biotechnology and materials are planned, with Ali also scheduled to conduct an in-orbit experiment involving photosynthetic cyanobacteria," The Times of India wrote today.

The third Shenzhou-23 crewmate, Zhu Yangzhu, will remain on the station until Shenzhou-24 comes home. Zhu will therefore set a Chinese record, becoming the first astronaut from his country to live in low Earth orbit for a full year.

In a recent development, astronauts from the Soviet Union/Russia and the United States have already blazed this long-duration trail. The global record for longest continuous space stay is 437 days, set by cosmonaut Valeri Polyakov aboard the Mir space station from January 1994 to March 1995.

Ali is not the first person from Pakistan ever to reach space, by the way. That distinction belongs to adventurer Namira Salim, who traveled to suborbital space on a tourism flight with Virgin Galactic in October 2023.

Shenzhou-24 is the 12th crewed mission to Tiangong, a three-module, T-shaped outpost that China finished assembling in late 2022. Well, "finished" might not be the right term; China plans to expand Tiangong, which is currently about 20% as massive as the International Space Station.
